Senator Ingvversen, Representative Meyer and members of the Health and Human Services
Committee:
My name is Butch Russell, and I am the Executive Director of the Maine Ambulance Association.
We appreciate the Legislature's commitment to EMS funding through the $31 million grant
allocation last session. However, both rounds of grants are already unden/vay, and EMS services
are actively receiving funds that are critical to their operations.
S0 those funds are no longer available to increase Mainecare rates. That said, we believe LD 35
presents an opportunity to advance the broader goal: the creation of a well-structured Medicaid
matching program to bring long-term sustainability to EMS funding in Maine.
We support LD 35 with amendment--specifically, to establish a fair and effective EMS~focused
Medicaid match program.
Timeline of efforts leading to this opportunity
in 2022, the first Blue Ribbon Commission to Study Emergency Medical Sen/ices was convened to assess the financial condition of EMS across Maine. In its final report, released in December 2022, the Commission found a $70 million annual funding shortfall and recommended the development of a Medicaid supplemental payment program, including a provider assessment model and intergovernmental transfers.
In 2023, LD 1751 was introduced to implement these recommendations. The bill proposed establishing the program to draw down nearly $20 million in federal matching funds through EMS provider assessments and municipal transfers. After discussion in the Health and Human Services Committee, LD 1751 was amended to a resolve directing MaineCare to study the feasibility of a Medicaid supplemental payment program for EMS. The resolve was carried over to

the 2024 legislative session, but was never funded by the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee. Despite broad stakeholder support and two years of Commission findings, the initiative was left incomplete.
In 2023, a second Blue Ribbon Commission was convened and issued an updated report in January 2024, that reaffirmed and expanded on the previous recommendations. The Commission again emphasized that a Medicaid match program using EMS-generated funds could bring
meaningful, long-term financial sustainability to sen/ices statewide with minimal reliance on the General Fund.
In January 2025, an Medicaid match program for ambulances was proposed as PartTl' of the
Governor's budget LD 210. It proposes a 6% tax on about 50 non-governmental ambulance
sen/ices, which would be matched with federal Medicaid funds. However, it redirects about half
of these new funds to unrelated MaineCare shortfalls, and it directs the EMS portion of the new funds to raise the rates of over 200 EMS providers. This creates the inequitable problem between
taxed ambulances services that would lose money, and the untaxed sen/ices would gain a
windfall. Accordingly, this Health and Human Sen/ices Committee voted Ought Not to Pass on LD
210, Part Ti in its report to the Appropriations Committee. There is little support on either side of
the aisle for a proposalthat harms EMS providers to balance the broader MaineCare budget.
LD 35 is the Opportunity to Create an EMS Medicaid Match Program that would
help ambulances and the Mainecare budget
We recommend amending LD 35 to do the following:
1. Direct DHHS to create a Medicaid supplemental payment program for all ambulances 0 An assessment program for non-governmental services up to 6% of patient revenue 0 An intergovernmental transfer (IGT) option for municipal EMS providers
2. Cap the supplemental payments to the Average Commercial Rate, as required by federal
law.
3. Use any remaining funds for Mainecare budget needs.
We respectfully urge the Committee to support LD 35 with this amendment to establish a durable
funding model that meets the urgent needs of our EMS providers and the communities they sen/e.
Thank you for your continued support of emergency medical services in Maine.
Butch Russell Executive Director
Maine Ambulance Association

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services

April 17, 2025

Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Health and Human Services, my name is Chip Curry. I represent Senate District ll, which includes
the 26 rural, coastal, and island communities of Waldo County.

Today, I present to you LD 35, "An Act to Strengthen Local Emergency Medical Services by Increasing
the MaineCare Reimbursement Rate for Ambulance Services," and ask you to consider a sponsor's
amendment, which I have attached to my testimony. I understand this amendment was also shared with
the interested parties list. This amendment and the original bill share the same goal: to the greatest extent possible, federal funds should be brought in to fill the financial hole in Maine's Emergency Medical
System.
The Blue Ribbon Qommission on Maine EMS identified an annual gap in funding of somewhere between $70 and $90 million. The expenses of delivering EMS in the state simply overwhelm the revenues. These
costs have historically been absorbed by a volunteer corps and local philanthropy, but must increasingly
be covered by local property taxpayers. Today's proposal is designed to strengthen our EMS providers
and reduce the pressure on our local property taxpayers.
This committee has heard the amendment before. In May of 2023, I proposed LD I751, which was one
of the recommendations of the Blue Ribbon Commission on EMS.

This amendment replicates the provider assessment fee and the dedicated ambulance fund structure from
LD 1751. It would establish a provider assessment program to strengthen Maine's emergency medical
services system without increasing pressure on the General Fund. It does so by charging a modest, annual fee to non-municipal ambulance providers based on their operating revenue. The revenue collected is
then used to draw down additional federal Medicaid dollars, significantly increasing the reimbursement
rates those providers receive for delivering emergency services under MaineCare.

The amendment creates a dedicated, nonlapsing Ambulance Fee Fund where all collected fees, federal matching funds, and any future appropriations are held. These funds must be used solely to increase MaineCare reimbursement for emergency ambulance services and cannot replace existing General Fund support. To the extent funding allows, reimbursement rates can be increased up to the average
commercial rate ---- a substantial step forward in ensuring sustainability for providers.

10044946:
LD 35 - An Act to Strengthen Local Emergency Medical Services by Increasing the MaineCare Reimbursement Rate for Ambulance Services
Testimony in Support
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services:
My name is Joe Kellner of Windham, and I serve as the Chief Executive Officer of LifeFlight of Maine. I come before you today with substantial experience and background on reimbursement matters related to emergency medical services in Maine. I have served on two consecutive Blue Ribbon Committees on emergency medical services. My testimony today is on behalf of LifeFlight of Maine.
LD 35 creates a federal matching program for payments to emergency medical services that are not municipal or are not already part of a similar program through parent hospitals.
I support this approach because it remains impossible to break even on the provision of ambulance services in Maine through patient revenues for any service responding to 911 calls. The cost increases for many years have exceeded payment increases. Based on the size (volume) and rurality of a service, they will "lose" $150-$1,800 per call that they go on in provision of the service - this must be made up through supplemental revenue sources. Many services are now relying on per-capita fees, which have been the subject of many headlines here in Maine. CMS cost reporting data substantiates my estimates on the revenue to cost gaps.
Maximization of federal funds is good policy for Maine, while shielding impact to local taxation.
During language review, the committee should consider the exemption on air medical services, as there are no services that do exclusively air medical. LifeFlight is happy to be included in this initiative to the extent our participation adds value.
You may also note that there is a similar proposal, which we oppose, that takes the supplemental monies accreted through this program and allocates them away from ambulance services. We support this approach, as it keeps the money where it is needed most.
Thank you for your consideration.
-Joe

Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
Neither For Nor Against
LD 35, An Act to Strengthen Local Emergency Medical Services by Increasing the MaineCare Reimbursement Rate for Ambulance Services
April 17, 2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, my name is Rebecca Graham, and I am submitting testimony neither for nor against on behalf of Maine Municipal Association for LD 35, An Act to Strengthen Local Emergency Medical Services by Increasing the MaineCare Reimbursement Rate for Ambulance Services, at the direction of our 70 member Legislative Policy Committee (LPC).
As originally drafted, municipal officials supported the increased reimbursements that are also linked to private insurance reimbursements and artificially below the true cost of providing the services. As amended last night, the bill gives us pause for some truly important reasons already articulated in testimony provided under LD 210.
The amended version of the bill mirrors a budget proposal in LD 210 Part TT which does not include ambulance services paid for by municipal appropriation in a regional manner through interlocal agreements. This conflicts with other state driven policy to regionalize services particularly in rural areas where ambulance services do not receive the call volume necessary to support anything more than a regional emergency response approach.
Communities in many areas of Maine have accomplished the challenging work of bringing multiple communities together to create a regional response owned and paid for by all their municipalities. This work has been further incentivized by other state policy to appropriate funds for community informed processes and expand interlocal cooperation for emergency response and is in direct conflict with the list of exempted services in the amended version which appears to punitively tax the municipal appropriation for services most will not benefit from.
During testimony on this provision under LD 210 before the Appropriations Committee earlier this year, Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) Deputy Commissioner Mann testified that not all services would benefit from the taxation that would be assessed on their operations. In addition, because the department isn't working from a list of service providers that qualify for the tax or the reimbursement, it is impossible to determine how much

of the $5.3 million would go back to service providers and how much would go towards MaineCare operations. The potential increased reimbursement coming from the growth in the federal match is part of the selling point, but not everyone who pays to play will win.
In many cases interlocal services would be paying and not receiving the increase reimbursements because of the low numbers of MaineCare subscribers in their communities. These areas are frequently where the oldest population in the state reside, making them also the most unable to bear additional taxation passed through to the property tax. If the proposal should consider municipal funds as "revenue" communities would be faced with a double taxation scenario. Even if only the revenue received from emergency transport were to be taxed, communities would still be faced with the increased cost of the assessment, paid for with property taxes, with no guarantee of reimbursement.
Without amendment, the bill would create a scenario where the some of the poorest and oldest areas of the state are subsidizing this program for communities with far greater resources through a tax levy on their interlocal cooperation built to keep emergency services alive in their communities at great budget expense. We respectfully ask the sponsor and the committee to consider amending the language in �2150-M. 1 (B) to include interlocal agreements as exempted from the taxation.
B. A municipal fire or police department or any other governmental or interlocal agreement entity that provides emergency ambulance services;
Alternatively, the department could list the service providers that the new fee would pertain to directly and provide clarity as to which services this would impact which may provide a clearer picture of the fairness of the fee's application.
